title: Ukraine Peace Talks Resume in Abu Dhabi
summary:
Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia, and the United States have begun new talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending the war in Ukraine. Expectations for a breakthrough are low, but American officials said Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing 'a little bit of flexibility' about who would control Ukraine's eastern regions after the war.

Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the American delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff, said the talks would focus on the 'postwar security concerns' of both Russia and Ukraine. 'An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war,' Kushner wrote.

The biggest sticking point is Donetsk, a region in eastern Ukraine now mostly controlled by Russia. Moscow has demanded Ukraine give up the parts it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line and keep those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.

Neither side has budged in public, but an American official said the issue cannot be solved without first agreeing on a new 'security architecture' for after the war. For Ukraine, that could mean reassurance that allies would come to its aid if attacked again. For Russia, it could mean its longstanding wish to see NATO pull back from eastern Europe, a prospect that alarms Europeans.

The framework under discussion includes security consultations, crisis hotlines, and 'reciprocal de-escalation measures.' Officials also raised restarting the NATO-Russia Council, largely paused since 2022. The last round of talks, in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough.

European leaders, who have largely been left out, have pushed to be involved. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged that NATO allies and EU members be included, and the American side said it would propose bringing the Europeans into a wider format.
why_it_matters: The talks could shape how the war in Ukraine ends and how safe Europe is afterwards, so what is decided in Abu Dhabi matters far beyond the meeting room.

background_read: Peace talks are meetings where the sides in a war try to agree on how to stop the fighting and what should happen afterwards.
In talks like these, each side often wants land, safety promises, and a say in what happens after the war, and the hardest question is usually who controls the disputed land.
Countries also talk about security, which means promises and plans to keep everyone safe after the fighting stops, such as help from allies if one side is attacked again.
Other countries that are not at the talks often still care about the result, because a deal can change safety for a whole region.
